subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: In the classroom of the village school, Anand slid down in his seat with his cheek on his hand, eyes half shut, while Disha Ma'am talked about fractions. Disha Ma'am's mouth tightened. He's bored, or he doesn't care, she thought. She walked over and asked quietly, “Anand, are you all right?” He blinked. “Sorry, Ma'am. We were up all night. The buffalo had her calf.” Disha Ma'am's face softened. “Congratulations. Have some water and sit up when you can. We'll go through the fractions again after break.”

qa.q: What happened at Anand's home during the night?
qa.a: The buffalo had her calf.

qa.q: What did Disha Ma'am first think Anand's slouching meant, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: She first thought he was bored or did not care. It turned out he was tired from being up all night with the buffalo.

qa.q: What did Disha Ma'am do that treated the posture as a clue rather than proof?
qa.a: She walked over and asked quietly if he was all right, and then offered water and a chance to go through the fractions again.

qa.q: How might Anand have felt when Disha Ma'am came over?
qa.a: Perhaps worried that he was in trouble, and then relieved when she softened. He was probably tired and glad to explain.

grounding: Slouching in class may show tiredness rather than boredom; posture is a clue, not proof of attitude.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: In Ms Layla's class in Lisbon, Sofia slumped in her chair with her chin on her hand, staring at the ceiling. “Sit up, Sofia,” said Ms Layla. “We are learning about rivers.” Sofia straightened, but her eyes stayed on the ceiling. Ms Layla waited. After a moment Sofia said, “The river doesn't always flow to the sea. Sometimes it flows into a bigger river.” Ms Layla raised her eyebrows. “Yes. Good thinking.” Sofia looked pleased. “I think better when I lean.”

qa.q: What was Ms Layla teaching about?
qa.a: She was teaching about rivers.

qa.q: What did Ms Layla probably think about Sofia's slouch at first, and what else did it mean?
qa.a: She probably thought Sofia was not paying attention, then was pleasantly surprised when Sofia's answer showed she had been thinking hard. Ms Layla raised her eyebrows and said, "Good thinking."

qa.q: What could Ms Layla do next time she sees a slouch?
qa.a: Give a little time or ask a question first, since posture is a clue and not proof of attitude.

qa.q: How might Sofia feel about being told to sit up?
qa.a: Perhaps a bit misunderstood, since she was thinking. She still answered politely and seemed pleased when praised.

grounding: Slouching can be a comfortable way of thinking; posture is a clue, not proof of attitude.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: In the evening study hall at the boarding school, Kunal sat sprawled low in his chair, feet stretched out, chin almost on his chest, a physics book propped on his stomach. Lokesh Sir stopped beside him. “Kunal. Sit up. If you're bored, go to bed.” Kunal pushed himself upright. “I'm not bored, Sir. I'm on the magnets chapter. I think better leaning back.” Sir raised an eyebrow. “Tell me why a magnet sticks to the steel cupboard but not the wooden door.” Kunal answered, clearly. Sir nodded slowly. “All right. Lean back here. In class, though, other teachers will read it as not caring.” Kunal hadn't known that.

qa.q: Which chapter was Kunal reading?
qa.a: Kunal was on the magnets chapter.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when Sir asked if he was bored?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and a bit defensive, since he was concentrating and hadn't realised his slouch looked like boredom.

qa.q: How did Lokesh Sir check his first reading?
qa.a: He asked a question about the chapter, and Kunal's clear answer showed the slouch wasn't boredom.

qa.q: How do teachers often read a slouch like Kunal's?
qa.a: Many teachers read it as not caring or boredom, even when a student is actually thinking comfortably.

grounding: Shows a child learning that teachers read slouching as boredom, when it was a comfortable way of thinking.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Lalit, and I sit across the aisle from Nandini. This week she's been slumped over her desk every morning, shoulders rounded, head on her arm. On Wednesday Ma'am snapped, “Nandini, sit up, this is not a bedroom!” Nandini sat up, but a minute later she'd sunk down again. She's usually the first with her hand up. I don't know what's going on with her. But she also hasn't eaten her tiffin all week, and she doesn't laugh at Kiran's jokes anymore. At break I told Ma'am. Ma'am's face changed. She took Nandini for a walk round the garden, just the two of them, and later that day she called Nandini's mother.

qa.q: What has Nandini not eaten all week?
qa.a: Nandini hasn't eaten her tiffin all week.

qa.q: What might Nandini be feeling behind her slump?
qa.a: She might be tired or low and sad about something, since she has stopped eating and laughing; boredom seems less likely for someone usually first with her hand up.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that helped?
qa.a: Lalit told Ma'am about the other signs, which helped her see the slump as a clue to low mood and check in privately.

qa.q: How did Ma'am first read Nandini's posture?
qa.a: Ma'am first read it as laziness or boredom and told her to sit up, until Lalit's details changed her view.

grounding: Shows slouching read by a teacher as boredom when it may signal tiredness or low mood, and posture being a clue, not proof.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: Monday: In the first week of Ramzan, Asif sat slumped in the back row by afternoon, chin on his fist. Pema, beside him, thought he'd stopped caring about the science project they were doing together. She did the diagram alone, annoyed. Wednesday: At lunch Pema found Asif in the library instead of the canteen, head resting on a book. “Aren't you eating?” “I'm fasting till sunset. I get really tired after three.” Pema felt her face go hot. Friday: Pema moved their project work to the first period, when Asif sat up straight and full of ideas. By afternoon he could slouch, and she didn't mind.

qa.q: Until when is Asif fasting?
qa.a: Asif is fasting till sunset.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she did the diagram alone?
qa.a: Pema felt annoyed, thinking Asif's slump meant he had stopped caring about their project.

qa.q: What small change did Pema make, and why did it work?
qa.a: Pema moved their project work to the first period, when Asif had energy, so the tiredness no longer got in the way.

qa.q: What were those afternoons like for Asif?
qa.a: Asif was fasting and very tired after three, so his slouch came from low energy, not a lack of interest.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's slouch as not caring, and learning it came from tiredness, so posture is a clue, not proof.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: "Eshaan, sit however you like while you think. Let me, your Vidya Nani, tell you why. Thirty years ago I taught a boy called Mohan who slouched so low he was nearly under the desk. I was sure he was bored with my lessons, so I snapped at him in front of everyone: 'Sit up! This isn't your bed!' He sat up, went red and said nothing for a week. Then his mother came to see me. He had been helping at their dhaba until midnight every night. And you know what? Slouched in the next exam, he wrote the best essay in the class. I was wrong about him twice."

qa.q: Where had Mohan been helping until midnight?
qa.a: At their dhaba.

qa.q: What was Mohan likely feeling after Vidya snapped "Sit up!"?
qa.a: Embarrassed and hurt at being scolded in front of everyone; his reddening face and a week of silence show it.

qa.q: What choice in the story would have worked better than snapping?
qa.a: Vidya could have asked Mohan privately why he seemed so tired, instead of assuming the slouch meant boredom.

qa.q: How might Mohan's mother have felt coming to see the teacher?
qa.a: She likely felt worried for her son and wanted the teacher to understand that his tiredness came from late nights of work, not from boredom.

grounding: It is a retired teacher's memory of reading a pupil's slouch as boredom when it meant tiredness and, later, a comfortable way of thinking.
